script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Your research suggests that scientists have become worse at admitting uncertainty. Why do you think that is?

script.speaker: Scientist
script.text: I wouldn't say worse, exactly. The pressures have changed. Funding bodies and journalists want clear, confident messages, and a researcher who says 'we're not sure yet' risks sounding incompetent rather than honest.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: But surely the public wants clarity?

script.speaker: Scientist
script.text: Up to a point. The trouble is that when early, confident claims later turn out to be wrong – which is a perfectly normal part of science – people feel misled, and trust erodes. Paradoxically, being upfront about uncertainty from the start tends to make people more trusting in the long run, not less.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So scientists should hedge everything?

script.speaker: Scientist
script.text: No – endless hedging is just as unhelpful. The skill lies in being clear about what we know, what we suspect, and what we simply don't know yet.

items.question: Why, according to the scientist, do researchers avoid admitting uncertainty?
options: They are not allowed to by law.
The public never asks about it.
They fear appearing incompetent.
They are rarely uncertain.
items.explanation: '…a researcher who says "we're not sure yet" risks sounding incompetent rather than honest.'

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Your latest novel has been described as your most personal yet. Is that fair?

script.speaker: Author
script.text: It's funny – people always say that when a book is set somewhere I've lived. But the setting is the least personal thing about it. The town is real; the characters are entirely invented.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: So where does the personal element come from?

script.speaker: Author
script.text: From the questions the book is asking, I suppose. I wrote it the year after my father died, and although he isn't in it, every page is preoccupied with what we inherit from our parents – not money or property, but habits, fears, ways of seeing the world. I didn't plan that. I only noticed it when I reread the first draft.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Was that uncomfortable?

script.speaker: Author
script.text: Very. My first instinct was to cut half of it. Thankfully, my editor talked me out of it.

It refers to the real characters in the book.
items.explanation: She says the setting is the least personal thing; the personal element comes from the questions the book asks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Today I want to challenge a widespread assumption: that students learn best when material is presented in their preferred 'learning style' – visual, auditory and so on. It's an intuitively appealing idea, and surveys suggest the vast majority of teachers believe it. The problem is that when researchers have tested it properly – teaching students in their supposed style and then in a different one – the predicted benefit simply doesn't appear. Now, that doesn't mean all students are identical, or that variety in teaching is pointless. Quite the opposite. Most content is learned best in a particular way regardless of who's learning it: you learn geography from maps and music by listening. What matters is matching the method to the material, not to the student.

items.question: What does the lecturer say about research into learning styles?
options: It has never been carried out.
It shows visual learners perform best.
It has failed to show the expected benefits.
It has proved that learning styles are real.
items.explanation: '…the predicted benefit simply doesn't appear.'

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Electric cars are often presented as the solution to transport emissions. You're more cautious.

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: I'm cautious about the word 'solution'. Electric cars are clearly better than petrol cars in terms of emissions over their lifetime, especially as electricity grids get cleaner. I'm not disputing that.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: Then what's the concern?

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: That replacing every petrol car with an electric one leaves most problems untouched: congestion, the space cities give to parking, road deaths, even certain kinds of pollution from tyres and brakes. If we treat electric cars as the whole answer, we risk neglecting public transport, cycling and urban design, which tackle all of those at once.

script.speaker: Host
script.text: So you'd rather people didn't buy them?

script.speaker: Guest
script.text: Not at all. If you need a car, buy an electric one. I'm simply saying fewer cars should be the goal, not just cleaner ones.

options: They are no better than petrol cars.
They are an improvement but not a complete answer.
They should be banned in cities.
They will solve congestion.
items.explanation: 'Electric cars are clearly better… I'm cautious about the word "solution".'

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Have you seen the latest headlines? Apparently coffee now protects against heart disease. Last year it was supposed to cause it.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: That's exactly why I've stopped reading nutrition news. Every week there's a new miracle food or a new poison.

script.text: Do you think the research is just bad, then?

script.text: Not necessarily. A lot of it is observational – they notice that people who drink coffee have fewer heart problems, but those people might also exercise more or smoke less. The researchers usually acknowledge that; it's the headlines that turn 'is associated with' into 'causes'.

script.text: So who's to blame – scientists or journalists?

They exaggerate the risks of exercise.
They ignore observational research.
They report fake studies.
items.explanation: '…it's the headlines that turn "is associated with" into "causes".'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You've argued that we should be teaching children to be bored with technology, rather than excited by it. That sounds counterintuitive.

script.speaker: Expert
script.text: It's a deliberately provocative way of putting it. What I mean is that children are surrounded by devices designed to be thrilling – every notification, every reward is engineered to capture attention. If we only ever present technology as exciting, we reinforce that.

script.text: So what would 'boring' technology education look like?

script.text: Treating devices as tools rather than toys. Understanding how an app makes money, why a video platform recommends what it does, what happens to your data. Once you see the machinery behind the magic, it tends to lose some of its hold over you.

script.speaker: Presenter

Banning devices from schools.
Making lessons deliberately dull.
Encouraging children to avoid technology completely.
items.explanation: 'Treating devices as tools rather than toys… Once you see the machinery behind the magic…'

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Before we go in, a word about what you won't see. Visitors often ask why the museum displays so few objects relating to the workers who actually built this palace. The honest answer is that almost nothing survives. Their tools were reused until they broke; their homes were demolished; most couldn't write, so they left no letters. So as you admire the craftsmanship inside, I'd ask you to bear in mind that the history on display is, inevitably, a partial one, shaped by what was considered worth keeping.

The objects are kept in storage.
The museum chose not to display them.
items.explanation: 'The honest answer is that almost nothing survives.'

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Your company famously has no fixed holiday allowance. Employees can take as much as they like. Doesn't that get abused?

script.speaker: CEO
script.text: That was our fear too. In fact, the opposite happened. In the first year, people took fewer days off than before.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Why would that be?

script.speaker: CEO
script.text: Without a clear entitlement, people felt guilty taking time off, especially if their manager rarely did. Unlimited holiday turned out to mean no holiday at all for some people. We had to introduce a minimum – everyone must take at least twenty-five days – and managers are now expected to lead by example.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: So would you recommend the policy?

script.speaker: CEO
script.text: With reservations. The freedom is valuable, but only if the culture supports it. Otherwise it's just a nice-sounding policy that quietly works against the people it was meant to help.

items.question: What unexpected result did the unlimited holiday policy have?
options: Employees took far too many holidays.
Managers stopped working.
Some employees took less time off.
The company lost money.
items.explanation: 'In the first year, people took fewer days off than before.'

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: I volunteered at the food bank again on Saturday. The queue was longer than ever.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: It's admirable that so many people give up their time. It really shows the best of the community.

script.text: It does. But I've started to feel uneasy about how much we celebrate it.

script.text: Because in a wealthy country, the fact that people need food banks at all is a sign that something's gone wrong. When we praise the generosity of volunteers, we sometimes forget to ask why they're needed. Charity can end up masking a problem that ought to be addressed by policy.

script.text: Still, I'd rather people were fed by volunteers than not fed at all.

script.text: Absolutely – I'm not saying we should stop. I just think gratitude shouldn't replace questions.

The food bank is badly organised.
She thinks volunteers are not sincere.
Praising charity may distract from the causes of the problem.
items.explanation: 'When we praise the generosity of volunteers, we sometimes forget to ask why they're needed.'

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: It's often said that English has borrowed words from more languages than almost any other. That's broadly true, but it's worth looking at what kind of words get borrowed. Words for food, fashion and technology – things that travel with trade – cross borders easily. Words for basic concepts like 'water', 'hand' or 'mother' almost never do; they tend to stay remarkably stable over thousands of years. That's precisely why historical linguists use them to trace relationships between languages. If two languages share hundreds of words for computers, it tells you very little. If they share their words for body parts and family members, you may well be looking at distant relatives.

Words for food.
Words for fashion.
Words for technology.
items.explanation: 'Words for basic concepts like "water", "hand" or "mother" almost never do…'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You coach young athletes. What's the biggest mistake parents make?

script.speaker: Coach
script.text: Specialising too early. A parent sees a ten-year-old who's good at tennis and decides that's it – year-round training, no other sports. It seems logical: start early, get ahead.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: And it isn't?

script.speaker: Coach
script.text: For most sports, the evidence suggests not. Children who play a variety of sports tend to develop better all-round movement skills, get injured less and, crucially, are less likely to burn out and quit in their teens. Many elite athletes only committed to one sport surprisingly late.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Are there exceptions?

script.speaker: Coach
script.text: Gymnastics, perhaps, where peak performance comes young. But they're the exception, not the rule. My advice to parents is simple: let them play.

items.question: What does the coach see as the main mistake parents make?
options: Making children focus on a single sport too soon.
Choosing the wrong coach.
Not letting children play sport at all.
Pushing children to compete against adults.
items.explanation: 'Specialising too early.'

script.text: Your neighbourhood has changed enormously in the past decade. New cafés, galleries, rising rents. Do you welcome it?

script.text: It's complicated. I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy having a decent bakery round the corner. And the streets feel safer than they did.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: But?

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: But many of the people who made this area what it was can no longer afford to live here. The woman who ran the corner shop for thirty years had to close when her rent doubled. The irony is that the newcomers were attracted by the area's character – and that character is exactly what's disappearing.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Is there a solution?

script.speaker: Resident
script.text: I don't think you can stop change, nor should you. But protecting some affordable housing and small businesses would at least mean it wasn't only the wealthy who benefited.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's consider what's sometimes called 'decision fatigue' – the idea that the quality of our decisions deteriorates after we've made a lot of them. A famous study claimed that judges granted parole far more often early in the morning and just after lunch than late in the session. It was widely cited as evidence that even experts are worn down by decision-making. I'd urge some caution, however. Later analyses pointed out that the order of cases wasn't random – prisoners without lawyers, for instance, tended to be heard last, and their cases were less likely to succeed anyway. That doesn't mean decision fatigue is a myth. It means that a single striking study, however memorable, is rarely enough to settle a question.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Venice, Barcelona, Amsterdam – many cities are now actively discouraging tourists. As a travel writer, how do you feel about that?

script.speaker: Writer
script.text: Honestly, relieved. For years, my profession contributed to the problem – every article promising a 'hidden gem' helped to make sure it didn't stay hidden for long.

script.text: And what can travellers do?

script.text: Travel out of season, stay longer, and perhaps visit the places nobody is writing about – including, ironically, by ignoring writers like me.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: You served on a jury last year. What surprised you most?

script.speaker: Juror
script.text: How seriously everyone took it. I'd expected some people to be bored or to rush to a verdict so they could go home. Instead, we spent two days going through the evidence line by line.

script.text: So the verdict changed?

script.text: It did. I still don't know whether he did it. But I know we couldn't prove it – and that's what the system asks.

How little evidence there was.
How quickly the verdict was reached.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: On today's podcast, we're talking about reading. You've argued that we shouldn't feel guilty about abandoning books.

script.text: Absolutely. Many people force themselves to finish every book they start, as though giving up were a moral failing. Life's too short. If a book isn't working for you after fifty pages, put it down.

script.text: But aren't some of the greatest books difficult at first?

script.text: Certainly, and I'm not suggesting we only read what's easy. There's a difference between a book that's challenging and rewarding, and one that's simply not for you – or not for you yet. I abandoned one classic three times before I finally fell in love with it in my forties.

script.text: So timing matters?

script.text: Enormously. A book you hated at twenty can speak to you at fifty. Putting it down isn't the end of the relationship.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Discussions of climate change have traditionally focused on mitigation – reducing emissions to limit warming. Increasingly, though, attention is turning to adaptation: preparing for the changes that are already unavoidable. This shift was once controversial. Some campaigners feared that talking about adaptation would signal defeat and weaken the pressure to cut emissions. That concern hasn't entirely disappeared, but most experts now regard the two as complementary rather than competing. Coastal defences, drought-resistant crops and heat-proof buildings don't reduce the need to cut emissions; they simply acknowledge that some warming is already locked in. The real danger lies in pretending that one can substitute for the other.

It was too expensive.
It had already failed.

script.text: My company's started using AI to translate all our documents. It's saved a fortune on translators.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Is the quality good enough?

script.text: I can see why it sounds that way. But the evidence linking chronic loneliness to heart disease, depression and even early death is surprisingly robust – comparable, in some studies, to well-known risks such as smoking.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Is it mainly a problem for elderly people?

script.speaker: Researcher
script.text: That's the common assumption, but some of the highest rates we see are among young adults – people who've moved to a new city for work or study and haven't yet built a network. Being surrounded by people doesn't protect you; loneliness is about the quality of connections, not the quantity.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: What can be done?

script.speaker: Researcher
script.text: Interestingly, simply telling people to socialise more rarely works. What helps is creating situations where connection happens naturally – shared activities, community projects – rather than making loneliness itself the focus.

It only affects students.
It is very rare.
It is caused by social media.
items.explanation: '…some of the highest rates we see are among young adults…'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: As a film critic, how do you respond to people who say critics are out of touch with audiences?

script.speaker: Critic
script.text: Sometimes they're right. Critics see hundreds of films a year, so we can become impatient with familiar formulas that ordinary viewers genuinely enjoy.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So should critics simply reflect popular taste?

script.speaker: Critic
script.text: No – then there'd be no point in us. Audiences can already see what's popular from box-office figures. A critic's job is to explain why a film works or doesn't, to draw attention to films people might otherwise miss, and occasionally to make a case for something difficult.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Even if readers disagree?

script.speaker: Critic
script.text: Especially then. A good review isn't one you agree with; it's one that makes you think more carefully about why you disagree.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Generational labels – 'baby boomers', 'millennials', 'Generation Z' – have become a staple of journalism and marketing. They're convenient, but I want to suggest they obscure more than they reveal. Differences within a generation – by income, education, region – are typically far larger than differences between generations. A wealthy thirty-year-old and an unemployed thirty-year-old may have far less in common than the labels imply. There's also a tendency to confuse life stage with generation: young people have always been more likely to move house, change jobs and adopt new technology. When we attribute these behaviours to 'millennials', we mistake being young for belonging to a particular generation.

options: They are only used by marketers.
They hide important differences within each generation.
They are too difficult to define.
They exaggerate similarities between old and young.
items.explanation: 'Differences within a generation… are typically far larger than differences between generations.'

script.speaker: Man
script.text: I've been reading about the replication crisis in psychology. Apparently many famous findings couldn't be reproduced.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Yes, it's been quite a reckoning. When researchers repeated some classic experiments, a large proportion produced weaker results or none at all.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Doesn't that undermine the whole field?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: I'd argue the opposite, actually. The fact that psychologists themselves exposed the problem, and have changed their methods, shows science correcting itself, which is exactly what it's supposed to do.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: What kind of changes?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Researchers now often register their hypotheses before collecting data, so they can't quietly change them afterwards to fit the results. And journals are more willing to publish studies that find nothing – which used to be almost impossible.

items.question: What is the woman's view of the replication crisis?
options: It proves psychology is not a science.
It shows that science is able to correct its own errors.
It has been greatly exaggerated.
It has not led to any changes.
items.explanation: '…shows science correcting itself, which is exactly what it's supposed to do.'

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Your book argues that we should stop trying to be happy. That's a bold claim.

script.text: So what should we pursue instead?

It is deliberately provocative and not meant literally.

script.text: I've been asked to mentor a new graduate. I'm flattered, but I'm not sure what I'm supposed to do.

script.text: I mentored someone last year. My main mistake at first was trying to solve every problem she brought me.

Solving problems instead of helping his mentee learn to solve them.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: When we talk about the 'digital divide', we usually mean the gap between those who have internet access and those who don't. That gap is shrinking in many countries. But researchers increasingly describe a second-level divide: differences in how people use the internet once they're online. Two people with identical devices and connections may have very different experiences. One uses it to apply for jobs, manage finances and learn new skills; the other mainly for entertainment, perhaps because they lack the confidence or knowledge to do more. Closing the first divide is largely a question of infrastructure. Closing the second requires education and support, which is considerably harder and slower to deliver.

options: Differences in internet speed.
Differences in how people use the internet once they have access.
The gap between countries.
The cost of devices.
items.explanation: '…differences in how people use the internet once they're online.'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You've written a history of failure – inventions, expeditions and businesses that didn't work out. Why focus on failure?

script.speaker: Historian
script.text: Because history is usually written about the winners, which gives a distorted picture. We tend to see successful inventions as inevitable, when in fact many rivals were equally promising and failed for reasons that had nothing to do with quality – bad timing, poor funding, sheer bad luck.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Can you give an example?

script.speaker: Historian
script.text: Electric cars were actually quite popular in the early 1900s. They lost out to petrol not because they were worse in every respect, but because cheap oil was discovered and roads improved, making long-distance travel more important.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So failure is often a matter of circumstance?

script.speaker: Historian
script.text: Very often. Which should make us a little humbler about predicting which technologies will win today.

options: Most inventions are successful.

Successful inventions are poorly documented.
Focusing only on successes makes them seem inevitable.
items.explanation: 'We tend to see successful inventions as inevitable, when in fact many rivals were equally promising…'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Your city replaced a busy motorway with a park. Weren't people worried about traffic chaos?

script.speaker: Planner
script.text: Terrified. The predictions were apocalyptic – gridlock, businesses closing, commuters stranded.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: And what happened?

script.speaker: Planner
script.text: Something traffic engineers call 'traffic evaporation'. When road space is removed, a portion of the traffic simply disappears. People change their routes, travel at different times, switch to public transport or decide some journeys aren't worth making. It's the mirror image of what happens when you build new roads: they fill up almost immediately.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So the chaos never came?

script.speaker: Planner
script.text: There were a difficult few weeks. But within a year, traffic in the surrounding area was lower than before, and the park had become the most popular public space in the city. Frankly, I wish we'd been braver sooner.

items.question: What is 'traffic evaporation'?
options: Pollution disappearing from cities.
Traffic moving to new motorways.
Cars becoming more fuel-efficient.
A reduction in traffic when road space is removed.
items.explanation: 'When road space is removed, a portion of the traffic simply disappears.'

script.text: In principle, yes. Insects need far less land, water and feed than cattle. The logic is hard to argue with.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: In principle?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: In practice, I'd probably hesitate, and I'm not proud of that. It's purely cultural – billions of people around the world eat insects quite happily. We just grew up thinking of them as disgusting.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: So how would you persuade people like us?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Probably not by putting whole crickets on a plate. Grinding them into flour for pasta or bread seems to work better – people accept them once they're not recognisable. Over time, attitudes might shift, the way they did with sushi, which many Europeans once found revolting.

items.question: Why does the woman mention sushi?
options: To show that food attitudes can change over time.
To suggest insects taste like fish.
To explain why insects are popular in Japan.
To recommend a healthier alternative.
items.explanation: '…attitudes might shift, the way they did with sushi, which many Europeans once found revolting.'

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Economists have long debated why some countries grow rich while others remain poor. Geography plays a role – access to the sea, a temperate climate, natural resources. But natural resources can be a curse as well as a blessing. Several countries rich in oil or minerals have grown more slowly than resource-poor neighbours. One explanation is that easy revenue from resources reduces the incentive to develop other industries and makes governments less dependent on taxing their citizens – and therefore less accountable to them. Increasingly, economists emphasise institutions: secure property rights, independent courts and a government that is constrained by law. Without these, even abundant resources tend to benefit a narrow elite.

items.question: What does the lecturer mean by resources being 'a curse'?
options: Resources damage the environment.
Resources are too expensive to extract.
Resources are running out.
Resource wealth can slow wider economic development.
items.explanation: 'Several countries rich in oil or minerals have grown more slowly than resource-poor neighbours.'

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: You're a doctor who's become known for prescribing gardening, walking groups and art classes. Isn't that a bit unscientific?

script.speaker: Doctor
script.text: It's called social prescribing, and it's not as unconventional as it sounds. A large proportion of the patients I see aren't suffering from something a pill can fix. They're isolated, stressed or inactive, and that's affecting their health.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: But does it work?

script.speaker: Doctor
script.text: The evidence is still developing, and I'd be the first to admit some studies are small. But we do see reductions in GP visits and improvements in wellbeing. Most importantly, it gets people involved in their own recovery rather than passively receiving treatment.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: So medication is overprescribed?

script.speaker: Doctor
script.text: Sometimes. But I wouldn't put it that way. Medication is essential for many conditions. Social prescribing complements it; it doesn't replace it.

items.question: How does the doctor describe the evidence for social prescribing?
options: Entirely negative.
Encouraging, but still limited in some respects.
Conclusive and complete.
Non-existent.
items.explanation: 'The evidence is still developing, and I'd be the first to admit some studies are small.'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: As a fact-checker, do you think correcting false information actually changes people's minds?

script.speaker: Fact-checker
script.text: More often than people assume, though not always in the way you'd hope. There was a worry for some years about a 'backfire effect' – the idea that corrections make people cling to false beliefs even more strongly. Larger studies have found that's actually quite rare.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So corrections work?

script.speaker: Fact-checker
script.text: They shift beliefs about the specific facts. What they rarely shift is the attitudes behind them. Someone might accept that a particular statistic was wrong while remaining just as supportive of the politician who used it.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: That's rather depressing.

script.speaker: Fact-checker
script.text: Or realistic. Facts matter, but people's political loyalties are built on much more than facts.

items.question: What does the fact-checker say about the 'backfire effect'?
options: It was proved by recent research.
It only affects politicians.
Larger studies suggest it rarely happens.
It happens in most cases.
items.explanation: 'Larger studies have found that's actually quite rare.'

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: The new open-plan office was supposed to encourage collaboration. Has it?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: If anything, the opposite. People are wearing headphones all day to block out the noise, and important conversations have moved to messaging apps so others can't overhear.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: So face-to-face interaction has actually decreased?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That's what it feels like, and apparently there's research showing exactly that. When people lose privacy, they create it artificially.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Should we go back to separate offices, then?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: I wouldn't go that far. What seems to work best is variety – quiet areas for focused work, open spaces for meetings, and the freedom to choose. The mistake was assuming one layout would suit every task.

items.question: What has happened since the open-plan office was introduced?
options: Employees have found ways to recreate privacy.
Employees talk to each other more.
Productivity has doubled.
Collaboration has greatly improved.
items.explanation: 'People are wearing headphones all day… When people lose privacy, they create it artificially.'

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Bees are often held up as the symbol of declining insect populations, and rightly so. But I want to point out a common misunderstanding. When people hear 'save the bees', many think of honeybees, and some respond by keeping hives. Honeybees, however, are essentially farmed animals and are not endangered. In some areas, large numbers of hives can actually compete with wild bees for limited flowers, potentially making things worse for the species that genuinely are in decline. If you want to help, planting a variety of native flowers and leaving part of your garden untidy is likely to do far more good than buying a beehive.

items.question: What misunderstanding does the lecturer describe?
options: Believing that keeping honeybees helps endangered bees.
Thinking bees are not declining.
Thinking flowers harm bees.
Believing wild bees produce honey.
items.explanation: '…some respond by keeping hives. Honeybees, however, are… not endangered.'

script.speaker: Man
script.text: I've decided to stop flying for holidays. I'm going to take the train to Italy this summer.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: That's admirable, but won't it take forever?

script.speaker: Man
script.text: About a day and a half, with an overnight stop in Paris. I used to see the journey as wasted time, but now I see it as part of the holiday.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: I'd love to do that, but with two children and only two weeks off, it's just not realistic for us.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: I don't think it's realistic for everyone, and I'm not trying to make anyone feel guilty. Honestly, the bigger issue is how expensive trains are compared with budget flights. Until that changes, most people will keep flying.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: That's true. It shouldn't cost three times as much to do the right thing.

He prefers to travel overnight by plane.
He finds them more stressful.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: You've been learning Japanese for ten years. What's the hardest part?

script.speaker: Learner
script.text: People assume it's the writing system, and that's certainly a mountain to climb. But for me, it's the levels of politeness. The way you speak changes depending on who you're talking to – your boss, a customer, a friend – and getting it wrong can come across as rude or oddly distant.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: Do native speakers forgive mistakes?

script.speaker: Learner
script.text: Generally, yes – they're very patient with foreigners. But that's almost a problem in itself. Because they're so polite, they rarely correct you, so you can make the same mistake for years without realising.

script.speaker: Interviewer
script.text: How did you overcome that?

script.speaker: Learner
script.text: I asked a close friend to correct me ruthlessly. It was painful at first, but my Japanese improved more in six months than in the previous three years.

items.question: What does the learner find most difficult about Japanese?
options: Grammar rules.
Adjusting speech to different levels of formality.
Pronunciation.
The writing system.
items.explanation: '…for me, it's the levels of politeness.'

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: You've studied the effects of giving people cash with no conditions attached. What did you find?

script.speaker: Economist
script.text: The common fear is that people will waste it – on alcohol, gambling and so on. In the trials I've studied, that simply didn't happen on any significant scale. Most people spent it on food, school fees, tools or livestock.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: Did people stop working?

script.speaker: Economist
script.text: Very few. In some cases, they worked more, because they could finally afford to invest in a small business or travel to find better jobs.

script.speaker: Presenter
script.text: So why isn't it more widespread?

script.speaker: Economist
script.text: Partly politics. There's a deep-rooted belief that help should come with conditions and supervision. Ironically, monitoring how people spend money is often expensive and can cost more than it saves.

items.question: What did the economist find about how people spent the cash?
options: Most saved it all.
Most spent it on useful goods and investments.
Most wasted it on gambling.
Most gave it to relatives.
items.explanation: 'Most people spent it on food, school fees, tools or livestock.'

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: I went to that exhibition of AI-generated art at the weekend.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: And? Is it art?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: That's what everyone asks, and I think it's the wrong question. Some of the images were genuinely striking. But what I found more interesting was the debate around them – who the artist is when a machine produces the image.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: Surely it's the person who wrote the instructions?

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: Partly. But the system was trained on millions of images by human artists, most of whom were never asked or paid. So in a sense, they're uncredited collaborators.

script.speaker: Man
script.text: That sounds like a legal problem rather than an artistic one.

script.speaker: Woman
script.text: It's both. Questions about authorship have always been artistic questions too.

items.question: Why does the woman think 'Is it art?' is the wrong question?
options: The question has already been answered.
Nobody visited the exhibition.
The issue of authorship is more interesting.
The images were obviously not art.
items.explanation: '…what I found more interesting was the debate around them – who the artist is…'
